turns.prompt_text: In blackjack, how do you split?
turns.response_html:
In blackjack, splitting is a move you can make when your initial two-card hand consists of two cards of the same value (e.g., two 8s or two Kings). It allows you to turn one hand into two separate hands, each with its own bet.

How to Execute a Split

  1. The Signal: When it is your turn, place a second bet next to your original bet. The second bet must be equal to the first. In a casino, you should avoid touching the cards; instead, point with two fingers in a "V" shape to signal the split to the dealer.
  2. The Separation: The dealer will physically separate the two cards and deal a second card onto each.
  3. Independent Play: You now play each hand one at a time. You can hit, stand, or (depending on house rules) double down on these new hands.

Key Rules to Remember

  • Aces: When you split a pair of Aces, most casinos only allow you to receive one additional card for each hand. If that card is a 10-value card, it is usually counted as 21, not a "natural" Blackjack (meaning it pays 1:1 instead of 3:2).
  • 10-Value Cards: You can split any two 10-value cards (e.g., a Jack and a Queen), though this is generally considered a poor strategic move.
  • Doubling After Splitting (DAS): Check the house rules. Some tables allow you to double down on a hand after you have already split it; others do not.
  • Resplitting: If your new card creates another pair (e.g., you split 8s, and get another 8), many casinos allow you to split a third or even fourth time.

Basic Strategy: When to Split

While the choice is always yours, standard "Basic Strategy" suggests these guidelines to maximize your odds:

Always SplitNever SplitSplit Depending on Dealer Upcard
Aces (Increases your chance for two high hands)10s (You already have a strong 20; don't risk it)2s, 3s, and 7s (Usually split if the dealer shows a 2 through 7)
8s (16 is the worst hand in blackjack; splitting gives you a fresh start)5s (A total of 10 is better used for a Hit or Double Down)9s (Split if the dealer shows a 2 through 9, except for 7)

Note: Always check the specific table rules before you start, as variations in "re-splitting Aces" or "doubling after splits" can significantly affect the house edge.
